title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation fraud in which AI-generated content was used to fabricate a news interview featuring two real, named public figures, a finance presenter and a central bank governor, in order to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The failure did not originate inside a legitimate AI deployment. It is an adversarial use of AI tools by external actors to manufacture false credibility for a financial scam. The fabricated article gave the platform an air of journalistic legitimacy it had no right to claim.

The scale reported by ASIC, nearly nineteen and a half thousand scams removed in a single year with volume rising sharply, shows this is not an isolated event but a pattern of AI-assisted fraud applied systematically across multiple targets. The content was hosted on platforms that did not catch or remove it before it reached consumers. Detection would have required either platform-level screening for synthetic or impersonating content before publication, or rapid takedown mechanisms after publication, neither of which appears to have operated effectively here.

What is not established is whether any specific AI company or platform has been found liable, whether any individual behind this particular scam has been identified or prosecuted, and whether the numbers ASIC cites reflect all such scams or only those the regulator detected and acted upon.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featured a fabricated interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock discussing Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The article claimed Bullock became upset and walked out during questioning about the platform. This type of scam, using artificial intelligence to create deepfake content and false endorsements, is rapidly increasing in Australia according to the corporate regulator ASIC.

ASIC's recent research reveals investment scams have grown significantly, with the regulator removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. Scammers target well-known Australians including Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, businessman Dick Smith, and mining magnate Gina Rinehart by creating fake news articles, reviews, and websites to build credibility. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing, while presenter Kohler argues stronger penalties should apply to platforms hosting such content and the AI models generating it.
